There is a specific kind of silence that only exists between three and four in the morning, when even the people who stay up too late have finally given in, and the people who wake up too early haven't yet started their kettles. Inside the ferry terminal at Point Jude, that silence had a slight electrical buzz to it, courtesy of a vending machine selling stale peanut butter crackers and lukewarm cans of ginger ale.

I was sitting on one of those molded fiberglass benches bolted to the concrete floor—the kind designed to prevent anyone from getting too comfortable, though someone down at the far end had managed it anyway. He was curled around a canvas duffel bag, wearing a high-visibility jacket so faded the neon yellow had softened into the color of an old lemon. Every few minutes, he gave a sharp, dry snort, shifted his weight, and went right back under.

Outside the tall, salt-streaked windows, the water wasn't black so much as flat, like a sheet of slate pressed up against the pilings. You couldn't see the horizon. The fog had come in around midnight, thick and tasteless, swallowing the channel markers one by one until only the red beacon on the breakwater remained, blinking with the slow, indifferent patience of a lighthouse that had outlived everyone who cared about ships.

I had a thermos of coffee in my coat pocket and a paperback I'd already read twice, though I hadn't opened either. There is something strangely restorative about doing nothing in a public place before dawn. During the day, idleness feels like a mild failure, as if you're standing in the middle of a moving sidewalk and forcing everyone else to step around you. At 3:30 AM, nobody expects you to be productive. You are simply a warm shape occupying space until a boat arrives.

A moth was battering itself against the fluorescent tube above the ticket counter. *Tink, tink, tink.* Not frantic, just methodical, as if it were trying to knock on a door and hadn't realized nobody lived inside the glass. Behind the counter, the shutter was pulled halfway down, revealing a laminate desk cluttered with rubber bands, a dried-out highlighter, and a ceramic mug that read *WORLD'S OKAYEST DISPATCHER*. Someone had left a half-eaten glazed donut on a paper napkin beside a stack of laminated tide tables.

I thought about the person who worked that desk—probably someone who knew the names of half the islanders, who knew which cars belonged to the plumbers and which ones belonged to the summer people who only showed up in July with roof racks full of kayaks and dog hair on the upholstery. Every small port has an invisible ledger like that, kept in the heads of people who pour coffee at four in the morning and watch headlights sweep across empty parking lots.

My own reasons for being there were ordinary enough to be boring: a week of helping my sister clear out a rented garage in Providence, three days of rain that made the cardboard boxes smell like wet cellar stairs, and an old friend on the island who'd offered me a spare room and a few days of work re-shingling his porch roof. It was the kind of week made entirely of errands, the sort of time you don't really remember afterward except as a vague ache in your lower back and the memory of eating cold lo mein from a carton at midnight.

Yet sitting there, listening to the vending machine cycle its compressor with a shudder, I felt a sudden, sharp affection for the whole unglamorous machinery of getting from one place to another. We spend so much time trying to make our lives look intentional, smoothing over the gaps, pretending every transition has a neat arc. Most of life happens in waiting rooms, though—in hallways, in the five minutes while the radiator hisses, or in the gray hour before a five-thirty ferry docks.

Around four-fifteen, the glass door swung open and a burst of cold, briny air cut through the stale warmth of the terminal. A woman walked in pushing two plastic crates strapped to a hand truck. She wore thick rubber boots and a wool watch cap pulled low over her eyebrows. The man on the fiberglass bench stirred, squinted up at the ceiling, and sat up slowly, rubbing his palms over his face as if trying to wipe sleep off like water.

"Fog lifting at all?" he asked, his voice gravelly with disuse.

"Not yet," the woman said. She parked her hand truck near the double doors leading to the slip and leaned against the cinderblock wall, pulling a folded newspaper from her jacket. "Captain says it'll burn off by seven. Might be a slow crossing."

"Always is," he muttered, not unkindly.

That was the whole conversation. Nobody needed to embellish it. Twenty minutes later, headlights appeared out of the mist in the parking lot, sweeping across the terminal windows and illuminating dust motes suspended in the dead air. Then another pair. Then the shutter behind the ticket counter rattled upward with a metallic bang, and the dispatcher—a tall guy with a gray beard and a thermos twice the size of mine—stepped up to the glass, looked out at the three of us, and gave a single, brief nod.

Outside, faint against the rhythmic slap of water on wood, came the low, hollow groan of a horn. Not dramatic—just a sound announcing heavy iron moving slowly through fog. I unscrewed the lid of my thermos, poured a capful of coffee that had cooled from scalding to merely tolerable, and stood up to join the small, quiet line forming by the doors.
